examples.note: Describe a process in one tense and one voice throughout.

mistakes.wrong: Nowadays, people spent more time online than before.
mistakes.right: Nowadays, people spend more time online than before.
mistakes.explanation: Nowadays refers to the present, so the present simple is needed.

mistakes.wrong: In 2020 the figure has reached its highest point.
mistakes.right: In 2020 the figure reached its highest point.
mistakes.explanation: The present perfect cannot be used with a specific finished time.

mistakes.wrong: If technology will improve, costs will fall.
mistakes.right: If technology improves, costs will fall.
mistakes.explanation: The if-clause of a first conditional takes the present simple, not will.

mistakes.wrong: The report was published last year and describes three solutions.
mistakes.right: The report, which was published last year, describes three solutions.
mistakes.explanation: Placed side by side, the tense shift feels confused; a relative clause shows that the two time frames are deliberate.

mistakes.wrong: Since the last decade, air quality improved considerably.
mistakes.right: Over the last decade, air quality has improved considerably.
mistakes.explanation: Since is followed by a point in time (such as 2010); over is used for a length of time. In both cases the period is still running, so the present perfect fits.

keyTakeaways: Decide the time frame from the task, then stay in it.
A specific past time means past simple; since or no stated time means present perfect.
Describe what a chart or process shows in the present, and the data in the chart’s own time frame.
Every tense change needs a clear reason.

en.intro: Modals show how certain you are and how strongly you are recommending something. They do two main jobs: expressing how likely something is, and expressing what someone should do. Keeping these two jobs apart makes your argument sound balanced rather than one-sided.

rules.heading: Two jobs: likelihood and obligation
rules.rule: The same modal can express how likely something is (epistemic) or what is necessary (deontic). Context tells you which meaning is intended.
rules.whenToUse: Whenever you talk about the future, give advice or express an opinion.
structure: Possibility: This policy may reduce congestion. (it is possible)
Permission: Drivers may park here. (it is allowed)
Deduction: Costs must be rising, given the data. (I conclude this)
Obligation: Governments must act. (it is necessary)
notes: You do not need to memorise these terms; just get into the habit of asking yourself: am I talking about likelihood, or about what should be done?

rules.heading: Degrees of certainty
rules.rule: Modals can be arranged like a ladder, from almost certain down to a slight possibility. Choosing the right step keeps your claim reasonable.
rules.whenToUse: When you discuss an outcome you cannot prove.
structure: will - confident prediction: Demand will rise.
must - strong evidence-based deduction: The cause must be economic.
should - reasonable expectation: The scheme should reduce delays.
may / might / could - possibility: Automation may displace workers.
cannot - impossibility: This cannot be the only explanation.

rules.heading: Obligation and advice
rules.rule: Must is very strong and can sound like an order; should is the natural word for recommendations in an essay.
rules.whenToUse: In paragraphs that propose solutions.
structure: Governments should invest in renewable energy.
Schools ought to teach financial literacy.
Companies need to disclose their emissions.
Passengers must carry a valid ticket. (a rule, not an opinion)
Students do not have to attend. (no obligation)
notes: Must not means it is forbidden; do not have to means it is not necessary, but you may if you wish. They never mean the same thing.
In an argument, should is usually the better choice: it recommends without sounding like a law.

rules.heading: The modal rules that never change
rules.rule: A modal is always followed by the bare infinitive. Modals take no -s, no to after them, and two modals cannot sit side by side.
rules.whenToUse: Always.
structure: modal + base verb: should invest
modal + be + -ing: may be rising
modal + have + past participle: might have caused
modal + be + past participle: should be introduced
notes: should to invest, musts, will can and should invests are all impossible.
For past possibility, use might have + participle: The delay might have been caused by funding cuts.

examples.wrong: Governments must to reduce emissions.
examples.right: Governments must reduce emissions.
examples.note: A modal is followed by the bare infinitive.

examples.wrong: This policy will definitely solve all social problems.
examples.right: This policy could address several of these problems.
examples.note: A measured claim is far easier to defend than an extreme one.

examples.wrong: Students should to be encouraged to read widely.
examples.right: Students should be encouraged to read widely.
examples.note: Modal + be + past participle forms the modal passive.

examples.wrong: The rise might caused by population growth.
examples.right: The rise might have been caused by population growth.
examples.note: Past possibility takes might have been + participle.

examples.wrong: Employees must not work overtime if they do not want to.
examples.right: Employees do not have to work overtime if they do not want to.
examples.note: Must not means prohibition; do not have to means no obligation.

mistakes.wrong: The government should to introduce stricter laws.
mistakes.right: The government should introduce stricter laws.
mistakes.explanation: To never follows a modal.

mistakes.wrong: It will can solve the problem.
mistakes.right: It will be able to solve the problem.
mistakes.explanation: Two modals cannot sit together; replace the second with be able to.

mistakes.wrong: Technology must improves education.
mistakes.right: Technology must improve education.
mistakes.explanation: The verb after a modal never takes -s.

mistakes.wrong: Children may to watch television after finishing homework.
mistakes.right: Children may watch television after finishing homework.
mistakes.explanation: The same bare infinitive rule applies when the modal expresses permission.

mistakes.wrong: This evidence must proves that the theory is correct.
mistakes.right: This evidence suggests that the theory is correct.
mistakes.explanation: Besides the form error, must makes a stronger claim than a single piece of evidence can support.

keyTakeaways: Before choosing a modal, ask: am I expressing likelihood or obligation?
In essays, should is the natural way to recommend; keep must for rules and regulations.
Modal + bare infinitive: no to, no -s, never two modals together.
Use may, might and could to make claims you can genuinely defend.

en.intro: The passive is a tool for shifting focus. It moves the thing affected by an action into the subject position. You need it when the doer is unknown, obvious or unimportant. It is not a way to make writing sound weighty or scholarly; a paragraph written entirely in the passive becomes harder to read, not better.

rules.heading: How the passive is formed
rules.rule: The passive is be + past participle. Be carries the tense, so the participle never changes.
rules.whenToUse: When what was affected matters more than who did the action.
structure: Present simple: The data are collected annually.
Past simple: The scheme was introduced in 2015.
Present perfect: Several studies have been conducted.
Future: A new system will be installed.
Modal: Emissions should be reduced.
Continuous: The road is being widened.

rules.heading: Leaving out the agent
rules.rule: Include by + agent only when the reader needs to know who did the action. In academic writing it is usually omitted.
rules.whenToUse: In processes, research methods and general statements.
structure: Doer unknown: The documents were destroyed.
Doer obvious: The suspect was arrested. (by the police)
Doer irrelevant: The samples were stored at 4 degrees.
The doer is the key information: The theory was first proposed by Chomsky.
notes: In academic writing, roughly four out of five passives have no by-phrase.

rules.heading: Impersonal reporting
rules.rule: These two structures let you report a common view without naming who holds it.
rules.whenToUse: When summarising general opinion or established research in an essay.
structure: It + passive + that-clause: It is argued that automation will reduce employment.
Subject + passive + to-infinitive: Automation is believed to reduce employment.
Common verbs: argue, believe, claim, think, say, expect, consider, report, know.
notes: These are useful but very noticeable. Once or twice in an essay is enough.
The second structure needs a to-infinitive: X is believed to be..., never X is believed that...

rules.heading: When the active is better
rules.rule: Use the active when the doer is the point, or when the passive would hide responsibility or add needless words.
rules.whenToUse: Most of the time.
structure: Weak: It was decided by the committee that the project would be cancelled.
Better: The committee cancelled the project.
Weak: Mistakes were made.
Better: The department made several mistakes.
notes: In Task 2 the doers are usually clear: governments, schools, employers. Name them directly.

examples.wrong: The report was wrote by a team of researchers.
examples.right: The report was written by a team of researchers.
examples.note: The passive needs the past participle, not the past simple.

examples.wrong: The new policy will be introduce next year.
examples.right: The new policy will be introduced next year.
examples.note: After a modal, the structure is still be + past participle.

examples.wrong: It is believed that technology to improve productivity.
examples.right: It is believed that technology improves productivity.
examples.note: It is believed that is followed by a full clause.

examples.wrong: The glass is crushing and then melted.
examples.right: The glass is crushed and then melted.
examples.note: Process steps use the passive consistently.

examples.wrong: The problem was happened last year.
examples.right: The problem occurred last year.
examples.note: Intransitive verbs such as happen (which take no object) have no passive form.

mistakes.wrong: The results were showed in the second graph.
mistakes.right: The results were shown in the second graph.
mistakes.explanation: Shown is the participle; showed is the past simple.

mistakes.wrong: Many changes have been occurred since then.
mistakes.right: Many changes have occurred since then.
mistakes.explanation: occur, happen, rise, arrive and exist take no object, so they cannot be passive.

mistakes.wrong: It is said that the policy to be effective.
mistakes.right: The policy is said to be effective.
mistakes.explanation: Choose one structure: It is said that the policy is effective, or The policy is said to be effective.

mistakes.wrong: The decision was made by the government to increase the tax by them.
mistakes.right: The government decided to increase the tax.
mistakes.explanation: The passive added four extra words and forced the doer to be mentioned again. The active is clearer.

mistakes.wrong: Air pollution is effected by traffic volume.
mistakes.right: Air pollution is affected by traffic volume.
mistakes.explanation: Affect is the verb and effect is the noun. The passive structure itself was correct.

keyTakeaways: be + past participle; be carries the tense.
Drop the by-phrase if naming the doer tells the reader nothing new.
It is argued that... is useful, but use it sparingly.
When the doer matters, write in the active voice.

en.intro: Every verb is followed by a particular pattern: sometimes a gerund, sometimes an infinitive, sometimes object + infinitive, sometimes a that-clause. These patterns cannot be guessed from meaning, so you have to learn each verb together with its pattern. The good news is that a few dozen verbs cover almost everything you need in an essay.

rules.heading: Verb + gerund (-ing form)
rules.rule: Some common verbs are always followed by the -ing form, never by to.
rules.whenToUse: With verbs meaning avoid, continue, propose and consider.
structure: avoid, consider, suggest, involve, risk, delay, deny, mind, practise, enjoy, keep, finish
Governments should avoid raising taxes too quickly.
The plan involves building three new schools.
Critics suggest reviewing the policy.
notes: Suggest causes the most errors: suggest doing or suggest that someone do, but never suggest to do.

rules.heading: Verb + to-infinitive
rules.rule: Another group of verbs is followed by to + base form.
rules.whenToUse: With verbs of intention, tendency and attempt.
structure: tend, aim, fail, hope, plan, decide, attempt, refuse, manage, afford, offer, seek, choose
Young people tend to spend more time online.
The scheme aims to cut emissions by half.
Many countries have failed to meet their targets.

rules.heading: Verb + object + to-infinitive
rules.rule: Some verbs require a person or thing before the infinitive; this object cannot be left out.
rules.whenToUse: When someone causes or enables someone else to do something.
structure: allow, enable, encourage, force, require, persuade, advise, expect, cause, lead
Technology enables students to learn remotely.
The law requires companies to publish their emissions.
This allows people to work from home.
notes: You cannot write This allows to work from home. The object is compulsory.
Make and let take the bare infinitive: This makes people work harder.

table.caption: The patterns learners trip over most

rules.heading: Preposition + gerund and adjective + infinitive
rules.rule: A verb that comes directly after a preposition always takes the -ing form. Evaluative adjectives (important, difficult) are followed by a to-infinitive.
rules.whenToUse: In almost every complex sentence.
structure: preposition + -ing: interested in learning, capable of solving, responsible for managing
prevent / stop / discourage sb from doing
adjective + to-infinitive: difficult to measure, likely to increase, important to consider
It is + adjective + to-infinitive: It is essential to act now.
notes: The to in look forward to and be used to is a preposition, so it takes -ing: used to working late.
Note the difference: used to work means a past habit; be used to working means being accustomed to something.

examples.wrong: The report suggests to increase the budget.
examples.right: The report suggests increasing the budget.
examples.note: Suggest is followed by a gerund or a that-clause.

examples.wrong: This policy allows to reduce traffic.
examples.right: This policy allows cities to reduce traffic.
examples.note: Allow needs an object before the infinitive.

examples.wrong: They avoided to answer the question.
examples.right: They avoided answering the question.
examples.note: Avoid is always followed by -ing.

examples.wrong: The law prevents companies to pollute rivers.
examples.right: The law prevents companies from polluting rivers.
examples.note: The pattern for prevent is from + -ing.

examples.wrong: Students are capable to solve complex problems.
examples.right: Students are capable of solving complex problems.
examples.note: Capable is followed by of + -ing.

mistakes.wrong: I would recommend to study abroad.
mistakes.right: I would recommend studying abroad.
mistakes.explanation: Recommend follows the same pattern as suggest.

mistakes.wrong: The government should focus to improve healthcare.
mistakes.right: The government should focus on improving healthcare.
mistakes.explanation: Focus takes on, and a verb after a preposition must be -ing.

mistakes.wrong: Technology enables to communicate instantly.
mistakes.right: Technology enables people to communicate instantly.
mistakes.explanation: Like allow and require, enable needs an object.

mistakes.wrong: She is looking forward to hear from you.
mistakes.right: She is looking forward to hearing from you.
mistakes.explanation: This to is not part of an infinitive; it is a preposition, so -ing follows.

mistakes.wrong: It is difficult measuring happiness objectively.
mistakes.right: It is difficult to measure happiness objectively.
mistakes.explanation: After It is + evaluative adjective, use the to-infinitive.

keyTakeaways: Learn each verb and its following pattern together, as one package.
avoid, suggest, consider, involve and risk take -ing.
allow, enable, encourage and require need an object before to.
Any verb after a preposition takes -ing, even after look forward to.

en.intro: Which preposition to use depends on the word before it, not on logic. There is no explanation for why we say an increase in but an impact on; the pairs simply have to be remembered. They matter a great deal in Task 1: rose by and rose to describe two completely different numbers.

rules.heading: Noun + preposition
rules.rule: Academic nouns come with fixed prepositions. Learn the whole pair, not just the noun.
rules.whenToUse: In any sentence that expresses a relationship between two things.
structure: an increase / rise / fall / decline / reduction IN something
an impact / effect / influence ON something
access / solution / approach / damage TO something
a reason / need / demand FOR something
a lack / cause / risk OF something
a relationship / difference / link BETWEEN two things

table.caption: The pairs you need most
rows: the link between diet and illness

rules.heading: Verb + preposition
rules.rule: Many academic verbs must be followed by a particular preposition.
rules.whenToUse: When expressing cause, dependence and responsibility.
structure: result in / result from
depend on, rely on, focus on, concentrate on
contribute to, lead to, respond to, refer to
suffer from, benefit from, result from
deal with, cope with, associate with
notes: Result in introduces the effect; result from introduces the cause. Congestion results in pollution; pollution results from congestion.
discuss, mention, consider and affect take no preposition: write discuss the issue, not discuss about the issue.

rules.heading: Adjective + preposition
rules.rule: Adjectives have their own fixed prepositions too.
rules.whenToUse: In evaluative sentences.
structure: responsible for, suitable for, essential for
aware of, capable of, typical of, characteristic of
similar to, related to, due to, relevant to
different from, free from
concerned about, consistent with

rules.heading: Describing change in Task 1
rules.rule: Four patterns give four different kinds of information. Mix them up and you report the wrong number.
rules.whenToUse: Every time you describe a change in a figure.
structure: rise / fall BY - the size of the change: Sales rose by 20 per cent.
rise / fall TO - the final value: Sales rose to 80 million.
rise / fall FROM X TO Y: Sales rose from 60 to 80 million.
peak / stand / remain AT - a specific value: Sales peaked at 90 million.
notes: An increase of 20 per cent is the size of the rise; an increase to 20 per cent is where it ended up.

examples.wrong: There was a sharp increase of the number of tourists.
examples.right: There was a sharp increase in the number of tourists.
examples.note: Increase in says what rose; increase of says by how much.

examples.wrong: Social media has a huge impact in young people.
examples.right: Social media has a huge impact on young people.
examples.note: Impact always takes on.

examples.wrong: The figure rose to 20 per cent between 2000 and 2010, from 40 to 60 million.
examples.right: The figure rose by 20 per cent between 2000 and 2010, from 40 to 48 million.
examples.note: Use by for the size of the change and from... to... for the start and end values.

examples.wrong: Many countries are suffering of water shortages.
examples.right: Many countries are suffering from water shortages.
examples.note: Suffer takes from.

examples.wrong: The essay discusses about three solutions.
examples.right: The essay discusses three solutions.
examples.note: Discuss takes a direct object with no preposition.

mistakes.wrong: This leads to people become unemployed.
mistakes.right: This leads to people becoming unemployed.
mistakes.explanation: The to in lead to is a preposition, so the verb after it takes -ing.

mistakes.wrong: Unemployment is one of the main reasons of crime.
mistakes.right: Unemployment is one of the main reasons for crime.
mistakes.explanation: Reason takes for. The cause of crime would also work.

mistakes.wrong: The results are different than the ones reported in 2019.
mistakes.right: The results are different from the ones reported in 2019.
mistakes.explanation: Different from is standard in academic English; different than is mainly informal American usage.

mistakes.wrong: Consumption peaked to 90 million units.
mistakes.right: Consumption peaked at 90 million units.
mistakes.explanation: peak, stand and remain all take at.

mistakes.wrong: Students should concentrate in their studies.
mistakes.right: Students should concentrate on their studies.
mistakes.explanation: concentrate, focus, depend and rely all take on.

keyTakeaways: Memorise each noun with its preposition: increase in, impact on, access to.
Result in is followed by the effect; result from is followed by the cause.
discuss, affect, mention and consider take no preposition.
By = how much it changed; to = where it ended; at = a specific value.

en.intro: Academic Task 1 is comparison from start to finish, and Task 2 constantly asks you to weigh one option against another. Comparison errors cost twice: a wrong multiple (twice, three times) is not just poor language, it also reports the wrong data.

rules.heading: Comparative and superlative forms
rules.rule: One-syllable adjectives take -er and -est. Longer adjectives take more and most. Never use both together.
rules.whenToUse: Whenever you say which of two or more things is greater or smaller.
structure: One syllable: high - higher - the highest
Two syllables ending in -y: easy - easier - the easiest
Longer words: expensive - more expensive - the most expensive
Irregular: good - better - best; bad - worse - worst; far - further - furthest
notes: more higher and most highest are never correct.
Superlatives take the: the largest proportion.

rules.heading: Expressing equality and multiples
rules.rule: Use as + adjective + as for equality, and put the multiple (twice, three times) before the first as.
rules.whenToUse: When one figure is a multiple of another.
structure: as high as, not as high as
twice as many cars as
three times as expensive as
three times the number of cars
half as many visitors as

table.caption: Two ways to express a multiple

notes: Use many with countable nouns and much with uncountable nouns.
Do not write three times more than to mean three times as many as; three times more than is ambiguous.

rules.heading: Showing how big the difference is
rules.rule: An adverb placed before a comparative tells the reader how large the difference is.
rules.whenToUse: To add variety instead of repeating the same plain comparison.
structure: Large difference: significantly, considerably, substantially, far, much
Small difference: slightly, marginally, somewhat, a little
Examples: significantly higher, slightly more expensive, far less common
notes: very goes with plain adjectives, not comparatives: very high is fine, but write much higher.

rules.heading: Quantities, percentages and change
rules.rule: A figure can be expressed as a proportion, a fraction or a change. Each has its own pattern.
rules.whenToUse: Throughout Task 1.
structure: Proportion: 40 per cent of respondents; the proportion of women rose.
Fractions: a quarter of the sample; two thirds of all households.
Majority: the vast majority of; a small minority of.
Adjective + noun: a sharp rise, a slight decline, a steady increase, a dramatic fall.
Verb + adverb: rose sharply, fell slightly, increased steadily, declined dramatically.

table.caption: The same data, two structures
rows: There was a sharp rise in sales.
The graph shows a steady increase.

notes: Adjectives go before nouns; adverbs go after verbs. rose sharp and a sharply rise are clear errors.
A percentage of an uncountable noun takes a singular verb; a percentage of a plural noun takes a plural verb: 40 per cent of the water is..., 40 per cent of students are...

examples.wrong: The second city is more bigger than the first.
examples.right: The second city is much bigger than the first.
examples.note: Never combine more with an -er form.

examples.wrong: There were twice more visitors in July than in January.
examples.right: There were twice as many visitors in July as in January.
examples.note: Use as...as to express a multiple.

examples.wrong: Sales increased sharp between 2010 and 2015.
examples.right: Sales increased sharply between 2010 and 2015.
examples.note: An adverb describes the verb.

examples.wrong: The figure for Spain was the most highest of all.
examples.right: The figure for Spain was the highest of all.
examples.note: One superlative marker is enough.

examples.wrong: Three quarters of the energy are produced by coal.
examples.right: Three quarters of the energy is produced by coal.
examples.note: Energy is uncountable, so the verb is singular.

mistakes.wrong: China has the larger population in the world.
mistakes.right: China has the largest population in the world.
mistakes.explanation: Comparing one thing with all the others requires a superlative, not a comparative.

mistakes.wrong: Car ownership is higher than 1990.
mistakes.right: Car ownership is higher than it was in 1990.
mistakes.explanation: Compare like with like: a figure with a figure, not a figure with a year.

mistakes.wrong: There was a slightly increase in unemployment.
mistakes.right: There was a slight increase in unemployment.
mistakes.explanation: A noun is modified by an adjective, not an adverb.

mistakes.wrong: The number of users was more high in urban areas.
mistakes.right: The number of users was higher in urban areas.
mistakes.explanation: High is a short adjective, so it takes -er.

mistakes.wrong: Japan spent three times more money than Italy did on research.
mistakes.right: Japan spent three times as much money on research as Italy did.
mistakes.explanation: Three times more leaves it unclear whether you mean three or four times as much; the as...as pattern is precise.

keyTakeaways: Each adjective takes one comparative marker: either -er or more.
For multiples use twice / three times + as...as, or + the number of.
Adjective before a noun, adverb after a verb: a sharp rise, rose sharply.
Compare like with like, and make clear what you are comparing against.

en.intro: Band 7 and above requires complex sentences, but they only help when they are accurate. Almost every problem comes from two habits: expressing the same relationship twice (although and but together), or putting the wrong structure after a connector.

rules.heading: Three ways to join, three sets of rules
rules.rule: Coordinators (and, but, so) join two clauses of equal weight. Subordinators (because, although) make one clause depend on another. Linking adverbials (however, therefore) connect one sentence to the next.
rules.whenToUse: Whenever you connect two ideas.
structure: Coordinator: Clause, and clause. (and, but, so, or, yet, for, nor)
Subordinator: Although clause, clause. / Clause although clause.
Linking adverbial: Clause. However, clause. / Clause; however, clause.

table.caption: The same idea three ways
rows: The scheme was costly, but it worked.
Although the scheme was costly, it worked.
The scheme was costly. Nevertheless, it worked.

notes: Use exactly one of these three for each relationship. Using two is an error.

rules.heading: Choosing a subordinator by meaning
rules.rule: Choose the subordinator that expresses the relationship you intend; do not simply use the first one that comes to mind.
rules.whenToUse: While planning a complex sentence in your head.
structure: Reason: because, since, as
Result: so that, with the result that
Contrast: whereas, while
Concession: although, though, even though
Purpose: so that, in order that
Condition: if, unless, provided that, as long as
Time: when, while, before, after, until, once, as soon as

table.caption: Contrast vs concession
rows: Cities grew, whereas rural areas shrank.
Although funding rose, results did not improve.
Prices rose because demand outstripped supply.
Taxes were cut so that firms could invest.

notes: Whereas sets two facts directly against each other; although signals that the second fact is contrary to expectation.

rules.heading: Despite and in spite of take a noun
rules.rule: Despite and in spite of are prepositions, so they are followed by a noun, pronoun or -ing form, never a full clause.
rules.whenToUse: When you want to express contrast without writing another full clause.
structure: despite + noun: Despite the cost, the project continued.
despite + -ing: Despite costing millions, the project continued.
despite the fact that + clause: Despite the fact that it cost millions, the project continued.
although + clause: Although it cost millions, the project continued.
notes: Write despite, not despite of. In spite of is three separate words.

rules.heading: One relationship, one connector
rules.rule: Do not add a coordinator or adverbial that repeats the meaning of a subordinator already in the sentence.
rules.whenToUse: Check every sentence that contains although or because.
structure: Wrong: Although it is expensive, but it is effective.
Right: Although it is expensive, it is effective.
Right: It is expensive, but it is effective.
Wrong: Because of traffic, so people are late.
Right: Because of traffic, people are late.
notes: This is the most common complex-sentence error in IELTS writing, and it is entirely avoidable.

examples.wrong: Although the government increased spending, but the problem continued.
examples.right: Although the government increased spending, the problem continued.
examples.note: Although has already expressed the contrast.

examples.wrong: Despite of the high cost, the scheme was approved.
examples.right: Despite the high cost, the scheme was approved.
examples.note: Despite never takes of.

examples.wrong: Despite it was raining, the event continued.
examples.right: Although it was raining, the event continued.
examples.note: A clause needs although, not despite.

examples.wrong: Because the roads are congested, therefore commuting takes longer.
examples.right: Because the roads are congested, commuting takes longer.
examples.note: Because and therefore both express cause and effect; one is enough.

examples.wrong: Urban areas are growing, while rural areas are shrinking, however this is not universal.
examples.right: Urban areas are growing while rural areas are shrinking; however, this pattern is not universal.
examples.note: However needs a semicolon or full stop before it.

mistakes.wrong: Even though renewable energy is clean, but it remains expensive.
mistakes.right: Even though renewable energy is clean, it remains expensive.
mistakes.explanation: Even though is a subordinator, so it cannot be combined with but.

mistakes.wrong: In spite of the traffic was heavy, we arrived on time.
mistakes.right: In spite of the heavy traffic, we arrived on time.
mistakes.explanation: In spite of is followed by a noun phrase, not a clause.

mistakes.wrong: The policy failed, because of poor planning and it was underfunded.
mistakes.right: The policy failed because it was poorly planned and underfunded.
mistakes.explanation: Because of takes a noun and because takes a clause; mixing them breaks the sentence.

mistakes.wrong: Whereas some people prefer cities.
mistakes.right: Whereas some people prefer cities, others prefer the countryside.
mistakes.explanation: A whereas clause is dependent and cannot stand alone.

mistakes.wrong: Moreover, that the cost is high makes the scheme unpopular, and however it continues.
mistakes.right: The high cost makes the scheme unpopular. It continues nonetheless.
mistakes.explanation: Stacking connectors buries the actual argument. One clear relationship per sentence reads far better.

keyTakeaways: One relationship, one connector.
Although + clause; despite + noun or -ing.
Whereas shows a difference between two facts; although shows an unexpected result.
However and therefore need a full stop or semicolon before them.

en.intro: Relative clauses are the safest way to show complex structures in academic writing, because they add information about a noun without starting a new sentence. Getting them right takes two things: choosing the correct pronoun, and knowing whether the information is essential or just extra.

rules.heading: Choosing the right relative pronoun
rules.rule: The pronoun depends on what the noun is (a person, thing or place), not on its role in the sentence.
rules.whenToUse: Whenever you attach a clause to a noun.
structure: who - people: the students who attended
which - things: the policy which was introduced
that - people or things, defining clauses only
whose - possession: the company whose profits fell
where - places: the city where he was born
when - times: the year when the law changed
notes: That cannot be used in a non-defining clause: The report, that was published in 2020,... is wrong.
Which can refer to a whole clause: Sales fell, which worried investors.

rules.heading: Defining vs non-defining
rules.rule: A defining clause identifies exactly which one you mean and takes no commas. A non-defining clause adds extra information and is enclosed in commas.
rules.whenToUse: Decide which one you are writing before you place any commas, not afterwards.
structure: Defining: Students who study abroad often become more independent. (only those who study abroad)
Non-defining: My brother, who studies abroad, visits twice a year. (extra information)
Defining: The report that the committee published is controversial.
Non-defining: The report, which runs to 300 pages, is controversial.

table.caption: How the two types differ
rows: Yes, if it is the object

notes: Commas change the whole meaning. Workers who were unskilled lost their jobs means only the unskilled workers lost their jobs; Workers, who were unskilled, lost their jobs means all the workers were unskilled.

rules.heading: Do not add a second pronoun
rules.rule: The relative pronoun already fills the subject or object position, so no other pronoun can be added.
rules.whenToUse: Check every relative clause you write.
structure: Wrong: The policy which it was introduced reduced pollution.
Right: The policy which was introduced reduced pollution.
Wrong: The book that I read it was useful.
Right: The book that I read was useful.

rules.heading: Preposition + which, and reducing clauses
rules.rule: In formal writing, the preposition can move in front of which or whom. Defining clauses containing be can often be shortened.
rules.whenToUse: Fronting the preposition suits formal writing. Once you have mastered the full form, reduced clauses make sentences tighter.
structure: Informal: the problem which we are dealing with
Formal: the problem with which we are dealing
the rate at which temperatures are rising
the extent to which this is true
Reduced: The students who are enrolled on the course -> The students enrolled on the course
Reduced: The report which was published in 2020 -> The report published in 2020
Reduced: People who live in cities -> People living in cities
notes: Defining clauses with be, or with an active meaning, reduce easily.
Module 17 covers reduction in more detail, along with the dangling-modifier trap.

examples.wrong: The policy which it was introduced in 2015 reduced pollution.
examples.right: The policy which was introduced in 2015 reduced pollution.
examples.note: Which is already the subject here.

examples.wrong: My hometown which is in the north has grown rapidly.
examples.right: My hometown, which is in the north, has grown rapidly.
examples.note: The noun is unique, so the clause is non-defining and needs commas.

examples.wrong: The researcher that her study was published won an award.
examples.right: The researcher whose study was published won an award.
examples.note: Whose expresses possession.

examples.wrong: This is the village where I grew up in.
examples.right: This is the village where I grew up.
examples.note: Where already contains the preposition (where = in which).

examples.wrong: The report, that was released yesterday, criticises the plan.
examples.right: The report, which was released yesterday, criticises the plan.
examples.note: That cannot be used in a non-defining clause.

mistakes.wrong: Students which study hard usually succeed.
mistakes.right: Students who study hard usually succeed.
mistakes.explanation: Which is for things; people take who or that.

mistakes.wrong: The company, who employs 2,000 people, is expanding.
mistakes.right: The company, which employs 2,000 people, is expanding.
mistakes.explanation: An organisation is not a person, so it takes which.

mistakes.wrong: There are many reasons why people move to cities, which it is a global trend.
mistakes.right: There are many reasons why people move to cities, a trend seen worldwide.
mistakes.explanation: The extra it is wrong, and an appositive noun phrase is clearer here than another which.

mistakes.wrong: The period which the economy grew fastest was the 1990s.
mistakes.right: The period in which the economy grew fastest was the 1990s.
mistakes.explanation: The clause needs a preposition: in which, or simply when.

mistakes.wrong: People live in rural areas often have limited access to healthcare.
mistakes.right: People living in rural areas often have limited access to healthcare.
mistakes.explanation: A reduced clause needs the -ing form; otherwise the sentence has two finite verbs.

keyTakeaways: who for people, which for things, whose for possession.
If the clause identifies which one, no commas; if it adds extra information, use commas.
That is never used in a non-defining clause.
Never repeat the subject after a relative pronoun.

en.intro: A noun clause is a whole clause doing the job of a noun. It is how you report other people’s arguments, evaluate claims and structure an essay. The most common error here is keeping question word order inside an embedded question.

rules.heading: That-clauses
rules.rule: A that-clause can be the object of a reporting verb, or it can follow an adjective or noun to complete its meaning.
rules.whenToUse: When reporting what someone argues, shows or believes.
structure: As object: Critics argue that the policy is ineffective.
After an adjective: It is clear that demand has fallen.
After a noun: the claim that technology destroys jobs
As subject (rare, heavy): That the policy failed is undeniable.
notes: That can be dropped in informal writing, but it is better kept in academic writing.
Common reporting verbs: argue, claim, suggest, show, indicate, demonstrate, reveal, conclude, maintain.

rules.heading: Whether and if clauses
rules.rule: Use whether for yes/no alternatives. Whether is preferred to if in formal writing, and only whether can follow a preposition or come before to.
rules.whenToUse: When the clause represents a question that has not yet been answered.
structure: It is unclear whether the scheme will succeed.
The debate over whether tuition should be free continues.
They must decide whether to expand or consolidate.
whether or not: It will proceed whether or not funding is approved.
notes: You cannot write the question of if; only whether works after a preposition.

rules.heading: Embedded questions use statement word order
rules.rule: Once a question is embedded in a larger sentence, it behaves like a statement: no inversion and no auxiliary do.
rules.whenToUse: After wonder, explain, know, understand, show, examine and question.
structure: Direct: Why do people migrate?
Embedded: It is unclear why people migrate.
Direct: How can governments reduce waste?
Embedded: The report explains how governments can reduce waste.
Direct: Is the policy effective?
Embedded: Researchers question whether the policy is effective.
notes: Remove do, does and did completely, and return the main verb to its normal form.

rules.heading: Extraposition: moving the clause to the end
rules.rule: A that-clause or to-infinitive in subject position makes a sentence top-heavy. Move the clause to the end and start with it.
rules.whenToUse: In topic sentences and evaluative sentences.
structure: Heavy: That the climate is changing is now undisputed.
Extraposed: It is now undisputed that the climate is changing.
Heavy: To measure happiness accurately is difficult.
Extraposed: It is difficult to measure happiness accurately.
Useful frames: It is clear / likely / apparent / widely accepted / worth noting that...
notes: This is the same end-weight principle (heavy material last) that Module 20 applies to whole paragraphs.

examples.wrong: I wonder why do people move to cities.
examples.right: I wonder why people move to cities.
examples.note: Embedded questions use statement word order.

examples.wrong: The study examines how does air pollution affect health.
examples.right: The study examines how air pollution affects health.
examples.note: Remove does and put the -s back on the main verb.

examples.wrong: It is not clear that or not the policy will work.
examples.right: It is not clear whether the policy will work.
examples.note: Yes/no alternatives take whether.

examples.wrong: That the government should act is obvious to everyone who reads the data.
examples.right: It is obvious to everyone who reads the data that the government should act.
examples.note: Extraposition moves the heavy clause to the end.

examples.wrong: Researchers have discussed about whether the method is reliable.
examples.right: Researchers have discussed whether the method is reliable.
examples.note: Discuss takes no preposition.

mistakes.wrong: Nobody knows what will be the outcome.
mistakes.right: Nobody knows what the outcome will be.
mistakes.explanation: In an embedded clause the subject comes before the verb, so the outcome goes first.

mistakes.wrong: The question of if students should pay fees is controversial.
mistakes.right: The question of whether students should pay fees is controversial.
mistakes.explanation: Only whether can follow a preposition.

mistakes.wrong: It is argued the technology has reduced employment.
mistakes.right: It is argued that technology has reduced employment.
mistakes.explanation: Keep that in formal writing; it shows the reader where the new clause begins.

mistakes.wrong: Researchers want to know that why the figure fell.
mistakes.right: Researchers want to know why the figure fell.
mistakes.explanation: Do not combine that with a wh-word; one connector is enough.

mistakes.wrong: It is depends on whether funding is available.
mistakes.right: It depends on whether funding is available.
mistakes.explanation: This it is pattern is followed by an adjective, not a full verb.

keyTakeaways: Use verb + that-clause to report other people’s arguments.
Yes/no alternatives take whether, and only whether follows a preposition.
Embedded questions use statement word order and no auxiliary do.
Move heavy subject clauses to the end and begin the sentence with it.

en.intro: Conditionals are the grammar of argument. A paragraph proposing a solution is often one long conditional: if this were done, that would happen. Three structures do almost all of this work, and the core rule is simple: no will in the if-clause.

rules.heading: The three conditionals you need most
rules.rule: The zero conditional expresses general truths, the first conditional a realistic future, and the second conditional an imagined situation.
rules.whenToUse: Zero for general truths, first for realistic proposals, second for hypotheticals.
structure: Zero: If + present simple, present simple. If water reaches 100 degrees, it boils.
First: If + present simple, will + base. If governments invest in rail, congestion will fall.
Second: If + past simple, would + base. If governments invested in rail, congestion would fall.

table.caption: Which one to use when
rows: If demand rises, prices will increase.
If demand rose, prices would increase.

notes: The second conditional is not about the past; it is about an imagined present or future, even though the verb looks past.
In formal writing, were is used with all subjects, including I, he, she and it: If the policy were introduced...

rules.heading: No will in the if-clause
rules.rule: In the condition, the present simple carries future meaning. Will belongs only in the result clause.
rules.whenToUse: In every first conditional you write.
structure: Wrong: If the government will reduce taxes, businesses will invest.
Right: If the government reduces taxes, businesses will invest.
Right: If the government were to reduce taxes, businesses would invest.
notes: The same rule applies to when, as soon as, until and before: When prices rise, demand will fall.

rules.heading: Unless, provided that, as long as
rules.rule: Unless means except if, so it already contains a negative. Provided that and as long as express a condition that must be met.
rules.whenToUse: To vary your conditionals and to state the conditions under which a proposal will work.
structure: Unless action is taken, emissions will continue to rise.
The scheme will succeed provided that it is properly funded.
Remote work is effective as long as teams communicate regularly.
In the event of a shortage, prices would rise.
notes: Do not write unless... not: Unless the government does not act contains a double negative.
Provided that and as long as are also followed by the present tense, like the first conditional.

rules.heading: Conditionals in argument
rules.rule: Use the first conditional for proposals you consider realistic and the second for ones you want to present as hypothetical. Your choice reveals your position.
rules.whenToUse: In solution and opinion paragraphs.
structure: Realistic proposal: If schools introduced financial education, students would manage money better.
Consequence of inaction: Unless cities expand public transport, congestion will worsen.
Acknowledging a limit: Even if funding were doubled, the problem would persist.
notes: Mixed and third conditionals are useful but optional. Getting the first three right matters far more.

examples.wrong: If the government will invest more, the problem will be solved.
examples.right: If the government invests more, the problem will be solved.
examples.note: The if-clause takes the present simple.

examples.wrong: If people would recycle more, less waste would go to landfill.
examples.right: If people recycled more, less waste would go to landfill.
examples.note: The if-clause of a second conditional takes the past simple.

examples.wrong: Unless we do not act now, the situation will worsen.
examples.right: Unless we act now, the situation will worsen.
examples.note: Unless already means if not.

examples.wrong: If I was the minister, I would increase funding.
examples.right: If I were the minister, I would increase funding.
examples.note: Formal hypotheticals use were.

examples.wrong: The plan will work provided that it will receive support.
examples.right: The plan will work provided that it receives support.
examples.note: Provided that follows the same rule as if.

mistakes.wrong: If companies would pay higher wages, employees will be more motivated.
mistakes.right: If companies paid higher wages, employees would be more motivated.
mistakes.explanation: The sentence mixes two patterns. Use either past simple with would, or present simple with will.

mistakes.wrong: When the government will introduce the law, protests will begin.
mistakes.right: When the government introduces the law, protests will begin.
mistakes.explanation: Time clauses, like if-clauses, do not take will.

mistakes.wrong: If education would be free, more people could attend university.
mistakes.right: If education were free, more people could attend university.
mistakes.explanation: Would does not go in the condition; use were for a hypothetical.

mistakes.wrong: Unless if the policy changes, the issue will remain.
mistakes.right: Unless the policy changes, the issue will remain.
mistakes.explanation: Unless and if cannot be used together.

mistakes.wrong: If the scheme was introduced last year, results will appear soon.
mistakes.right: If the scheme was introduced last year, results should appear soon.
mistakes.explanation: A real past condition pairs better with a modal of expectation (such as should) than with a confident prediction.

keyTakeaways: Zero for general truths, first for a realistic future, second for hypotheticals.
Never put will in an if-clause or a time clause.
Unless already means if not, so do not add another not.
Your choice of conditional tells the reader how realistic you think a proposal is.

en.intro: Parallelism means keeping the parts joined by and, or or but in the same grammatical form. It works quietly: when it is right, nobody notices, but when it is wrong, a carefully built long sentence collapses at the end.

rules.heading: Keep every item in a list the same form
rules.rule: Each item in a list must be the same type: all nouns, all -ing forms, all infinitives or all finite verbs.
rules.whenToUse: In every sentence that contains a list of two or more items.
structure: All finite verbs: The policy reduces pollution, saves money and improves health.
All -ing forms: The scheme involves building schools, training teachers and funding equipment.
All nouns: The report examines cost, feasibility and public support.
All infinitives: The aim is to reduce waste, to cut costs and to raise awareness.
notes: With infinitives, either write to before every item or only before the first. Do not mix the two.

rules.heading: Paired connectors
rules.rule: Both sides of a correlative pair (both...and, either...or) must have the same structure.
rules.whenToUse: With not only...but also, both...and, either...or and neither...nor.
structure: both + X and + X: both in schools and in workplaces
not only + X but also + X: not only cheaper but also faster
either + X or + X: either raising taxes or cutting spending
neither + X nor + X: neither practical nor affordable

table.caption: Balancing both sides of the pair
rows: not only cheap but also it saves time
not only cheap but also time-saving
both for students and for teachers
either by taxation or by regulation

notes: Whatever word type (verb, noun, adjective) follows not only must also follow but also.

rules.heading: Parallelism in comparisons
rules.rule: The two sides of a comparison must be the same kind of thing.
rules.whenToUse: With than, as...as and numerical comparisons.
structure: Wrong: The population of Japan is larger than Canada.
Right: The population of Japan is larger than that of Canada.
Right: Japan has a larger population than Canada does.
Wrong: Reading is more useful than to watch television.
Right: Reading is more useful than watching television.
notes: Use that of (singular) and those of (plural) to refer back to the head noun without repeating it.

rules.heading: A shared word must fit every item
rules.rule: If the items in a list share a preposition, article or auxiliary, it must fit each item. If it does not, write the correct word separately.
rules.whenToUse: In long lists where one preposition is carrying several items.
structure: Wrong: The policy is interested in and committed to reform. (check that both sides fit)
Right: The policy shows an interest in and a commitment to reform.
Wrong: Students can apply for and benefit from the scheme at any time.
Right: Students can apply for the scheme and benefit from it at any time.

examples.wrong: The policy reduces pollution, saving money and to improve health.
examples.right: The policy reduces pollution, saves money and improves health.
examples.note: Three finite verbs in a row.

examples.wrong: She enjoys reading, to travel and cooking.
examples.right: She enjoys reading, travelling and cooking.
examples.note: Enjoy takes -ing, so every item takes the -ing form.

examples.wrong: The city is not only crowded but also it is expensive.
examples.right: The city is not only crowded but also expensive.
examples.note: An adjective on both sides of the pair.

examples.wrong: The climate of Spain is warmer than Norway.
examples.right: The climate of Spain is warmer than that of Norway.
examples.note: Compare climate with climate, not with a country.

examples.wrong: Governments should invest in education, improving healthcare and to build housing.
examples.right: Governments should invest in education, improve healthcare and build housing.
examples.note: All three items after should are now bare infinitives.

mistakes.wrong: The course teaches students how to write reports, giving presentations and research skills.
mistakes.right: The course teaches students how to write reports, give presentations and conduct research.
mistakes.explanation: All three items now follow how to as bare infinitives.

mistakes.wrong: He is responsible for planning, to organise events and the budget.
mistakes.right: He is responsible for planning events, organising budgets and managing staff.
mistakes.explanation: For is a preposition, so every item after it takes the -ing form.

mistakes.wrong: Neither the cost nor the benefits was clear.
mistakes.right: Neither the cost nor the benefits were clear.
mistakes.explanation: With neither...nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject, which is plural here.

mistakes.wrong: The report is both detailed and it is well researched.
mistakes.right: The report is both detailed and well researched.
mistakes.explanation: Both...and joins two adjectives here, not an adjective and a clause.

mistakes.wrong: Wages in the north are lower than the south.
mistakes.right: Wages in the north are lower than those in the south.
mistakes.explanation: Those in means wages in, so both sides of the comparison match.

keyTakeaways: Items joined by and or or must share the same form.
Whatever follows not only must also follow but also.
Use that of and those of to keep both sides of a comparison the same.
Read each list item separately with the start of the sentence to check it fits.

en.intro: Participle clauses merge two clauses into one, and they are a real sign of control over the language. They carry one big risk: if the doer of the participle is not the subject of the main clause, the sentence says something you never meant.

rules.heading: Reducing relative clauses
rules.rule: The pronoun and be can be removed from a defining relative clause. Use -ing for an active meaning and -ed for a passive meaning.
rules.whenToUse: To make noun phrases shorter and tighter without losing information.
structure: who are living in cities -> living in cities
which was published in 2020 -> published in 2020
that is causing concern -> causing concern
who have been affected -> affected

table.caption: Full form and reduced form
rows: People who live in rural areas
The report which was issued last week
Students who are enrolled on the course

rules.heading: Adverbial participle clauses
rules.rule: An -ing clause at the start or end of a sentence can express time, reason or result. The reader assumes the subject of the main clause is doing the -ing action.
rules.whenToUse: To combine two actions by the same doer in one sentence.
structure: Time: Having completed the survey, the researchers analysed the data.
Reason: Facing rising costs, many firms reduced staff.
Result: Demand fell sharply, causing prices to drop.
Passive: Introduced in 2015, the scheme has halved waiting times.
notes: Having + past participle shows that the action was complete before the main verb.
A result -ing clause at the end of a sentence is very useful in Task 1: The figure peaked in 2008, reaching 90 million.

rules.heading: Dangling modifiers
rules.rule: The doer of the participle must be the subject of the main clause. Otherwise the modifier dangles: it has nothing to attach to.
rules.whenToUse: Check every sentence that starts with an -ing or -ed form.
structure: Dangling: Walking to school, the rain started.
Fixed: Walking to school, I was caught in the rain.
Fixed: While I was walking to school, it started to rain.
Dangling: Having studied the data, the conclusion was obvious.
Fixed: Having studied the data, the researchers reached an obvious conclusion.
notes: The easiest fix is to write a full clause with a subordinator (when, because, after).
This error is hard to spot because the sentence sounds fluent. Ask yourself: who is actually doing the -ing action?

rules.heading: Adding information with an infinitive after a noun
rules.rule: A to-infinitive after a noun expresses purpose or what needs to be done.
rules.whenToUse: To shorten relative clauses that express purpose.
structure: the best way to reduce emissions
the first country to introduce the ban
a decision to be made by the committee
measures to be taken in the next decade
notes: If the action is done to the noun, use a passive infinitive: the issues to be addressed.

examples.wrong: Walking to school, the rain started.
examples.right: Walking to school, I was caught in the rain.
examples.note: The rain was not walking.

examples.wrong: Having finished the report, the deadline was met.
examples.right: Having finished the report, the team met the deadline.
examples.note: The deadline did not finish the report.

examples.wrong: The students enrolling on the course last year have graduated.
examples.right: The students enrolled on the course last year have graduated.
examples.note: The students were enrolled, so the passive -ed form is correct.

examples.wrong: Based on the data, it can conclude that demand is rising.
examples.right: Based on the data, we can conclude that demand is rising.
examples.note: The clause needs a subject for the participle to attach to.

examples.wrong: The figure rose steadily, reached a peak in 2010.
examples.right: The figure rose steadily, reaching a peak in 2010.
examples.note: A result clause takes the -ing form, not a finite verb.

mistakes.wrong: After reviewing the evidence, the policy was changed.
mistakes.right: After reviewing the evidence, the committee changed the policy.
mistakes.explanation: A passive main clause almost always creates a dangling modifier, because the real doer disappears from the sentence.

mistakes.wrong: Living in a big city, the cost of housing is very high.
mistakes.right: For those living in a big city, the cost of housing is very high.
mistakes.explanation: The cost does not live anywhere; write about the people who do.

mistakes.wrong: The report writing by the committee was published yesterday.
mistakes.right: The report written by the committee was published yesterday.
mistakes.explanation: The report was written, so the reduced form needs the past participle.

mistakes.wrong: Being a developing country, the government cannot afford this.
mistakes.right: Because it is a developing country, my country cannot afford this.
mistakes.explanation: A government is not a country; writing a full clause resolves the mismatch.

mistakes.wrong: Introducing in 2015, the scheme has reduced waiting times.
mistakes.right: Introduced in 2015, the scheme has reduced waiting times.
mistakes.explanation: The action is done to the scheme, so a passive participle is needed.

keyTakeaways: -ing for active meaning, -ed for passive meaning.
The subject of the main clause must be the doer of the participle.
If it is not, write a full clause with a subordinator.
In Task 1, a result -ing clause at the end of a sentence is safe and useful.

en.intro: Academic writing sounds academic not because of long chains of clauses, but because it packs a lot of information into noun phrases. Building noun phrases, and unpacking them when needed, is the most useful advanced skill in this course. Knowing where to stop is part of that skill.

rules.heading: Four ways to expand a noun phrase
rules.rule: Description can be added before the noun, after it, or on both sides. All four patterns are used heavily in academic writing.
rules.whenToUse: When a sentence feels loose or keeps repeating itself.
structure: Adjective + noun: rapid growth
Noun + noun: government policy, traffic congestion, air quality
Noun + of-phrase: the growth of the economy
Noun + another preposition: the impact on rural communities
Noun + relative or participle clause: the policy introduced in 2015

table.caption: Building a noun phrase step by step
rows: rapid population growth in coastal cities
rapid population growth in coastal cities driven by migration

notes: In noun + noun combinations, the first noun stays singular: a three-year programme, a car park, government policy.

rules.heading: Nominalization (turning verbs into nouns)
rules.rule: Nominalization turns a verb or adjective into a noun. This lets a whole process become the subject of a sentence (prices rose → the rise in prices).
rules.whenToUse: When you want to refer back to an action concisely, or make it the topic of the next sentence.
structure: rise -> the rise; grow -> growth; decide -> the decision
reduce -> a reduction; expand -> expansion; analyse -> analysis
Because prices rose rapidly, demand fell. -> The rapid rise in prices reduced demand.
The government decided to invest. -> The government decision to invest...
notes: The adverb becomes an adjective: rose rapidly becomes a rapid rise.
Keep the noun’s fixed preposition: a rise in, an impact on, a reduction in.

rules.heading: Apposition and noun complement clauses
rules.rule: In apposition, two noun phrases sit side by side and the second renames the first. A noun complement clause uses that to state the content of nouns such as idea, claim or fact.
rules.whenToUse: To explain a term without a new sentence, or to state what a claim actually says.
structure: Apposition: Jakarta, the capital of Indonesia, is sinking.
Apposition: One solution, congestion charging, has proved effective.
Noun + that-clause: the claim that technology destroys jobs
Common nouns: the idea / belief / fact / claim / argument / possibility that...
notes: A noun complement clause is not a relative clause: the fact that prices rose is correct; the fact which prices rose is not.

rules.heading: Knowing where to stop
rules.rule: Density is a tool, not a goal. When three or more modifiers pile up in one noun phrase, the reader has to unpack it piece by piece and the writing becomes unclear.
rules.whenToUse: When you lose track while rereading your own sentence.
structure: Overloaded: Government urban transport infrastructure investment policy reform proposals
Clearer: proposals to reform government policy on investment in urban transport
Overloaded: The implementation of the reduction of the utilisation of plastic
Clearer: Reducing plastic use
notes: A chain of of-phrases is a sure sign you have gone too far. Module 23 shows how to fix it.

examples.wrong: Because the population grew quickly, the city expanded.
examples.right: Rapid population growth drove the expansion of the city.
examples.note: The clause has become a noun phrase that can act as the subject.

examples.wrong: There was an increase of 20 per cent in the prices rapidly.
examples.right: There was a rapid 20 per cent increase in prices.
examples.note: Inside a noun phrase, the adverb becomes an adjective.

examples.wrong: the governments policies on the environment
examples.right: government environmental policy
examples.note: Noun modifiers stay singular and take no apostrophe.

examples.wrong: The fact which the policy failed is undeniable.
examples.right: The fact that the policy failed is undeniable.
examples.note: A noun complement clause takes that, not which.

examples.wrong: The reduction of the amount of the consumption of water
examples.right: Reduced water consumption
examples.note: Three of-phrases have been reduced to two noun modifiers.

mistakes.wrong: The increasing of prices has affected low-income families.
mistakes.right: The increase in prices has affected low-income families.
mistakes.explanation: When an established noun form exists, use it, together with its own preposition.

mistakes.wrong: a five-years plan for the development of the economy
mistakes.right: a five-year economic development plan
mistakes.explanation: Compound modifiers stay singular, and an adjective is lighter than an of-phrase.

mistakes.wrong: The analyse of the data shows a clear pattern.
mistakes.right: The analysis of the data shows a clear pattern.
mistakes.explanation: Analyse is the verb; analysis is the noun.

mistakes.wrong: There is a possibility of that the scheme will fail.
mistakes.right: There is a possibility that the scheme will fail.
mistakes.explanation: A noun complement clause follows the noun directly; no preposition comes before that.

mistakes.wrong: The utilisation of the implementation of new technology methodologies
mistakes.right: Introducing new technology
mistakes.explanation: Stacking abstract nouns destroys meaning. When that happens, go back to a verb.

keyTakeaways: Arrange information before and after the head noun.
Turning a clause into a noun phrase lets a whole process become the subject.
Noun modifiers stay singular: a three-year plan, government policy.
If the reader has to read it twice, stop there.

en.intro: Hedging is how experienced writers make claims they can defend. An absolute claim with all or always immediately makes the reader think of an exception, but a measured claim survives. Hedging is not weakness or vagueness; it is saying precisely as much as your evidence supports.

rules.heading: The hedging toolkit
rules.rule: Four kinds of words can soften a claim: modal verbs, lexical verbs (tend, appear), adverbs (often, generally) and quantifiers (many, some).
rules.whenToUse: In any general claim about causes, effects or the future.
structure: Modal: may, might, could, can, would
Verb: tend to, appear to, seem to, suggest, indicate, imply
Adverb: often, generally, largely, arguably, relatively, possibly
Quantifier: many, most, some, a number of, in some cases
Frames: It is likely that..., It appears that..., There is evidence that...

table.caption: Softening a claim
rows: This suggests that the theory holds.
Pollution is a significant contributor to illness.

rules.heading: Add a condition instead of a hedge
rules.rule: Often the best approach is not to soften the verb, but to state the circumstances in which the claim holds.
rules.whenToUse: When you believe the claim, but it is not true in every case.
structure: Weak: Technology always improves education.
Better: Technology can improve educational outcomes when it is properly implemented.
Better: In well-resourced schools, technology has improved outcomes considerably.
notes: A conditional clause does not just soften the claim; it makes it more precise.
It also strengthens your Task Response, because it shows you have considered limitations.

rules.heading: Reporting what others say
rules.rule: Your choice of reporting verb reveals your own stance, so choose it deliberately.
rules.whenToUse: When referring to research, critics or common opinion.
structure: Neutral: states, reports, notes, describes
Supportive: shows, demonstrates, establishes, confirms
Cautious: suggests, indicates, implies
Distancing: claims, asserts, alleges
notes: With shows or demonstrates you accept the finding yourself; suggests or indicates carries no such commitment.
Claims signals that you doubt the point. Use it on purpose, not by accident.

rules.heading: Do not over-hedge
rules.rule: Stacking hedges until the sentence says nothing is as bad as overclaiming. One or two per claim is enough.
rules.whenToUse: When editing your writing.
structure: Over-hedged: It could possibly be argued that there may perhaps be some evidence that this might be true.
Fixed: There is some evidence that this is true.
Over-hedged: It seems that it may be likely that costs could rise.
Fixed: Costs are likely to rise.
notes: In IELTS Task 2 you must answer the question. Hedging measures your position; it is not an excuse for not having one.

examples.wrong: Technology always improves education.
examples.right: Technology can improve educational outcomes when it is implemented effectively.
examples.note: Adding a condition makes the claim defensible.

examples.wrong: All young people are addicted to social media.
examples.right: Many young people spend a considerable amount of time on social media.
examples.note: Both the absolute quantifier and the overstated verb have been changed.

examples.wrong: This study proves that exercise prevents depression.
examples.right: This study indicates that exercise may help prevent depression.
examples.note: A single study indicates; it does not prove.

examples.wrong: It is possible that it might perhaps be true that costs may rise.
examples.right: Costs are likely to rise.
examples.note: One hedge is enough.

examples.wrong: Everybody knows that cities are dangerous.
examples.right: Cities are often perceived as less safe than rural areas.
examples.note: Present an opinion as an opinion, not as established fact.

mistakes.wrong: Pollution definitely causes all respiratory diseases.
mistakes.right: Pollution contributes to a range of respiratory conditions.
mistakes.explanation: All and definitely are impossible to defend; contributes to describes a realistic relationship.

mistakes.wrong: The graph proves that the policy was successful.
mistakes.right: The graph suggests that the policy had some effect.
mistakes.explanation: A chart shows a trend; it does not prove a cause.

mistakes.wrong: It tends to be that students may possibly perform better.
mistakes.right: Students tend to perform better.
mistakes.explanation: Tend to is already a hedge; the rest is padding.

mistakes.wrong: In my opinion, I think that perhaps the government should maybe act.
mistakes.right: The government should act.
mistakes.explanation: Your position should be clear. Hedge claims about evidence, not your own opinion.

mistakes.wrong: Research is proving that this approach is the only solution.
mistakes.right: Research suggests that this approach is one effective solution.
mistakes.explanation: The only solution is an absolute claim that no research can support.

keyTakeaways: Use modals, tend to, suggest and adverbs to match the claim to the evidence.
Adding a condition is often better than softening the verb.
Reporting verbs carry your stance: shows commits you, suggests does not.
One hedge per claim; do not hedge your own position out of existence.

en.intro: Writing flows when each sentence starts with something the reader already knows. When a paragraph feels disjointed, most people add more linking words. The real fix is usually to change the order of information inside the sentence.

rules.heading: Given before new
rules.rule: Start a sentence with what the reader already knows, and put the new information at the end.
rules.whenToUse: In every sentence after the first one in a paragraph.
structure: Choppy: A new tax was introduced in 2015. Congestion fell by 20 per cent because of the tax.
Flowing: In 2015 the city introduced a new tax. This measure cut congestion by 20 per cent.
notes: Readers remember the last few words of a sentence best. Put your key point there.
This principle does most of the work you are trying to make linking words do.

rules.heading: End-weight
rules.rule: Long, complex material goes at the end of the sentence, not at the start.
rules.whenToUse: When the subject grows longer than about ten words.
structure: Heavy subject: That governments should invest more heavily in renewable infrastructure is clear.
End-weight: It is clear that governments should invest more heavily in renewable infrastructure.
Heavy subject: The need to reduce emissions, cut waste and protect biodiversity is urgent.
End-weight: There is an urgent need to reduce emissions, cut waste and protect biodiversity.

rules.heading: Tools for reordering information
rules.rule: Four structures let you move information around a sentence without changing the information itself.
rules.whenToUse: When writing the sentence the natural way puts the new information first.
structure: Passive: brings the affected thing forward. The scheme was criticised by residents.
Existential there: introduces something new. There are three explanations for this.
Extraposition: moves a clause to the end. It is clear that demand has risen.
Fronted adverbial: sets the context first. In rural areas, access remains limited.
notes: These are the same structures from Modules 8 and 14, used here for flow rather than for grammar.

rules.heading: Linking sentences: this + summary noun
rules.rule: Start a sentence with this or these plus a noun that sums up the previous sentence in one word.
rules.whenToUse: At the start of a sentence that comments on the whole previous sentence.
structure: Cities are expanding rapidly. This expansion places pressure on housing.
Many firms now allow remote work. This shift has reduced office demand.
Useful nouns: trend, shift, change, approach, measure, finding, problem, development, practice.
notes: This is both a cohesion technique and a way of putting given information first.
Without a noun, this on its own is often unclear. Modules 4 and 21 make the same point.

examples.wrong: A sharp fall in rainfall, which affected three regions and lasted two years, occurred.
examples.right: There was a sharp fall in rainfall, which affected three regions and lasted two years.
examples.note: The heavy material is now at the end of the sentence.

examples.wrong: Firstly, cities grew. Moreover, housing costs rose. Furthermore, commuting increased.
examples.right: Cities grew rapidly. This growth pushed up housing costs and lengthened commutes.
examples.note: Reordering removed the need for three connectors.

examples.wrong: To find a solution that satisfies all stakeholders is difficult.
examples.right: It is difficult to find a solution that satisfies all stakeholders.
examples.note: Extraposition moved the heavy part to the end (end-weight).

examples.wrong: Residents criticised the scheme. The scheme was expensive and poorly planned.
examples.right: The scheme was criticised by residents, who considered it expensive and poorly planned.
examples.note: The passive brings the known topic to the front.

examples.wrong: Unemployment rose. This is a problem.
examples.right: Unemployment rose sharply. This increase has placed pressure on welfare budgets.
examples.note: The summary noun picks up the previous idea and carries it forward.

mistakes.wrong: Moreover, in addition, furthermore, the cost should also be considered.
mistakes.right: Cost is a further consideration.
mistakes.explanation: Three connectors are doing the same job of adding a point. The sentence order already does that.

mistakes.wrong: That the climate is changing rapidly and that action is needed urgently is accepted.
mistakes.right: It is widely accepted that the climate is changing rapidly and that urgent action is needed.
mistakes.explanation: Two heavy subject clauses belong at the end of the sentence.

mistakes.wrong: Congestion charging reduced traffic. Traffic reduction improved air quality. Air quality improvements reduced illness.
mistakes.right: Congestion charging reduced traffic, which improved air quality and, in turn, lowered rates of illness.
mistakes.explanation: Mechanically chaining given-new across three sentences sounds artificial; one sentence says it better.

mistakes.wrong: There is the government which should act on this issue.
mistakes.right: The government should act on this issue.
mistakes.explanation: Existential there introduces new, indefinite information, not a subject the reader already knows.

mistakes.wrong: This is why it matters a lot for the future.
mistakes.right: This pattern matters because it shapes long-term planning.
mistakes.explanation: The vague this is replaced with a summary noun and a reason, so the link is clear.

keyTakeaways: Start with information the reader knows; end with new information.
Put heavy material at the end of the sentence.
Use the passive, there, extraposition and fronting to reorder without changing content.
This + summary noun is the most reliable way to link two sentences.

en.intro: Cohesion is not a long list of connectors. It is the set of techniques that let a text point back to what it has already said without repeating it in full. The band descriptors explicitly penalise mechanical overuse of cohesive devices, which makes reference, substitution and ellipsis far more valuable skills.

rules.heading: Reference
rules.rule: Pronouns, demonstratives (this, these) and the definite article (the) all point back to something already mentioned.
rules.whenToUse: In every paragraph, all the time.
structure: Pronoun: The committee met yesterday. It approved the budget.
Demonstrative: Three cities were studied. These differ in size.
Definite article: A new tax was introduced. The tax raised 2 billion.
Comparative reference: a similar pattern, the same trend, another approach
notes: The alone tells the reader the noun has appeared before; it creates cohesion by itself.

rules.heading: Substitution
rules.rule: Instead of repeating a long phrase, replace it with a short word.
rules.whenToUse: When you would otherwise repeat a noun or verb phrase.
structure: one / ones for countable nouns: The old system was slow; the new one is faster.
do so / does so for verb phrases: Those who recycle do so for environmental reasons.
so for clauses: If demand rises, and it seems likely to do so, prices will follow.
such + noun: Such measures are rarely popular.
notes: Do so is the formal written version of do it, and it is very useful in essays.

rules.heading: Ellipsis
rules.rule: Leave out words the reader can recover from the previous clause.
rules.whenToUse: In paired structures and comparisons.
structure: Some countries invest heavily in rail; others, in roads.
The first policy succeeded; the second did not.
She can speak French, and he can too.
More was spent on healthcare than on education.
notes: The reader must be able to recover whatever you omit. If they would have to guess, write the words out.

rules.heading: Use connectors sparingly
rules.rule: Use a linking adverbial only when the relationship is genuinely unexpected or needs to be stated. Do not start every sentence with a connector.
rules.whenToUse: Roughly once every three or four sentences, not more.
structure: Overloaded: Firstly, cities are growing. Moreover, housing is scarce. Furthermore, prices are rising. In addition, wages are flat.
Natural: Cities are growing while housing remains scarce. Prices have risen accordingly, and wages have not kept pace.

table.caption: What to do instead of adding another connector
rows: Join the two sentences with and or a relative clause
Move forward with this + summary noun
Build a list inside one sentence
Use a result participle clause: ..., reducing costs.

examples.wrong: The new policy replaced the old policy because the old policy was ineffective.
examples.right: The new policy replaced the old one, which had proved ineffective.
examples.note: Substitution and a relative clause removed two repetitions.

examples.wrong: People who volunteer, they volunteer for personal reasons.
examples.right: People who volunteer usually do so for personal reasons.
examples.note: Do so replaces the whole verb phrase.
