examples.wrong: Firstly, pollution is rising. Secondly, traffic is rising. Thirdly, noise is rising.
examples.right: Pollution, traffic and noise are all increasing.
examples.note: One sentence does the work of three connectors.

examples.wrong: These kind of problems require urgent action.
examples.right: These kinds of problem require urgent action.
examples.note: These must agree with a plural noun.

examples.wrong: Some countries invest in rail. Other countries invest in roads.
examples.right: Some countries invest in rail; others, in roads.
examples.note: Ellipsis removes the words the reader can supply.

mistakes.wrong: Such problem is difficult to solve.
mistakes.right: Such problems are difficult to solve.
mistakes.explanation: Such is followed by a plural or uncountable noun; a singular countable noun needs such a.

mistakes.wrong: Moreover, furthermore, the cost is also high.
mistakes.right: The cost is also high.
mistakes.explanation: Also already adds the point, so the other two connectors are redundant.

mistakes.wrong: The report was long. This made difficult to read.
mistakes.right: The report was long, which made it difficult to read.
mistakes.explanation: Make needs an object; here it refers to the report.

mistakes.wrong: I prefer the first option than the second one.
mistakes.right: I prefer the first option to the second.
mistakes.explanation: Prefer takes to, and after ellipsis the second is enough on its own.

mistakes.wrong: Students who study abroad, they do it because of career reasons.
mistakes.right: Students who study abroad often do so for career reasons.
mistakes.explanation: Remove the extra pronoun and use the formal alternative do so.

keyTakeaways: Reference, substitution and ellipsis create cohesion without connectors.
Use one, ones, do so and such instead of repeating the same phrase.
Leave out only what the reader can recover.
A connector in every sentence sounds mechanical and costs marks.

en.intro: This module is optional. Clefts and inversion are real structures that skilled writers use for emphasis. But IELTS does not require them for any band, and many candidates who force inversion turn a correct sentence into an incorrect one. Learn them so you recognise them, and use them only when emphasis is genuinely needed.

rules.heading: What-clefts
rules.rule: A what-cleft moves the part you want to emphasise into the second half of the sentence.
rules.whenToUse: At most once per essay, usually to emphasise a central point or recommendation.
structure: Plain: Governments need long-term planning.
Cleft: What governments need is long-term planning.
Plain: The cost matters most.
Cleft: What matters most is the cost.
notes: When a what-clause is the subject, the verb after it is singular: What matters is...

rules.heading: It-clefts
rules.rule: An it-cleft singles out one particular part of the sentence, especially to show contrast.
rules.whenToUse: When correcting a reader’s likely misconception.
structure: Plain: Poor planning caused the delay.
Cleft: It was poor planning that caused the delay.
Plain: The policy failed in rural areas.
Cleft: It was in rural areas that the policy failed.
notes: Use that for things and circumstances, and who or that for people.

rules.heading: Negative inversion
rules.rule: When a sentence opens with a negative or restrictive adverbial such as never, rarely or only then, the subject and auxiliary swap places, as in a question.
rules.whenToUse: Rarely, and only when you fully control the structure.
structure: Not only does the scheme reduce costs, but it also improves safety.
Rarely has a policy attracted so much criticism.
Only after 2010 did the figure begin to fall.
Under no circumstances should this be ignored.

table.caption: Normal and inverted forms
rows: The scheme not only reduces costs but also improves safety.
Not only does the scheme reduce costs, but it also improves safety.
A policy has rarely attracted so much criticism.
Rarely has a policy attracted so much criticism.
The figure only began to fall after 2010.
Only after 2010 did the figure begin to fall.

notes: If there is no auxiliary, do, does or did fills the slot and the main verb returns to its base form.
In not only...but also, only the first clause inverts, not the second.

rules.heading: When not to use them
rules.rule: Emphatic structures have a cost: they are long, noticeable and easy to get wrong. A plain sentence never loses marks for being plain.
rules.whenToUse: Read this before using any structure from this module.
structure: IELTS rewards a range of structures used accurately and flexibly, not a checklist of particular 'impressive' forms.
An inverted sentence with errors does far more damage than an accurate plain sentence.
If a structure does not come easily and naturally under time pressure, do not use it in the exam.
notes: At advanced level, marks really come from the skills in Modules 18 to 21. Treat this module as extra knowledge.

examples.wrong: What governments needs is long-term planning.
examples.right: What governments need is long-term planning.
examples.note: The verb inside the what-clause agrees with governments.

examples.wrong: Not only the scheme reduces costs, but also improves safety.
examples.right: Not only does the scheme reduce costs, but it also improves safety.
examples.note: A fronted negative needs inversion, and the second clause needs its own subject.

examples.wrong: Rarely a policy has attracted so much criticism.
examples.right: Rarely has a policy attracted so much criticism.
examples.note: Rarely at the start triggers inversion.

examples.wrong: It was the cost what caused the delay.
examples.right: It was the cost that caused the delay.
examples.note: An it-cleft takes that, not what.

examples.wrong: Only after the law changed the figure began to fall.
examples.right: Only after the law changed did the figure begin to fall.
examples.note: Only + adverbial requires do-support and the base form.

mistakes.wrong: Never before people have had access to so much information.
mistakes.right: Never before have people had access to so much information.
mistakes.explanation: With a fronted negative, the auxiliary moves before the subject.

mistakes.wrong: What is needed are stronger regulations.
mistakes.right: What is needed is stronger regulations.
mistakes.explanation: The what-clause is a singular subject, so the verb stays singular.

mistakes.wrong: Not only it is expensive but also ineffective.
mistakes.right: It is not only expensive but also ineffective.
mistakes.explanation: If you do not front the phrase, no inversion is needed; the normal form is correct and simpler.

mistakes.wrong: Under no circumstances we should ignore this evidence.
mistakes.right: Under no circumstances should we ignore this evidence.
mistakes.explanation: A fronted restrictive phrase requires inversion.

mistakes.wrong: It is the government who is responsible for it is the funding.
mistakes.right: The government is responsible for funding.
mistakes.explanation: No cleft is better than a broken one. When in doubt, write the plain sentence.

keyTakeaways: These structures are optional and not required for Band 8.
What-clefts and it-clefts shift the emphasis; keep the verb singular after a what-clause.
A fronted negative inverts the subject and auxiliary, with do-support where needed.
An accurate plain sentence always beats an impressive sentence with errors.

en.intro: This module introduces no new grammar; it is an editing checklist. Everything here happens after the writing is done: cutting what is unnecessary, placing modifiers next to the right word, and keeping subjects close to their verbs. These habits reduce errors even under exam pressure, because short, well-organised sentences contain fewer mistakes.

rules.heading: Cut the deadwood
rules.rule: Some familiar phrases only add length, not meaning. Replace them with a single word.
rules.whenToUse: In every draft, even when you only have two minutes left in the exam.
structure: due to the fact that -> because
in spite of the fact that -> although
at this point in time -> now
in the event that -> if
has the ability to -> can
a large number of -> many
in order to -> to
it is important to note that -> can often be deleted entirely

table.caption: Long form and short form
rows: There are many people who believe
The reason why this happens is because

notes: Nouns made from verbs often hide the real action: write decide instead of make a decision. When the nominalization from Module 18 goes too far, this is how you turn it back into a verb.

rules.heading: Keep the subject close to the verb
rules.rule: When many words separate a subject from its verb, the reader has to hold the subject in mind, and the risk of agreement errors rises.
rules.whenToUse: When more than about eight words come between the subject and the verb.
structure: Hard: The policy, which was introduced in 2015 after a lengthy consultation involving several agencies, failed.
Better: The policy failed, despite a lengthy consultation involving several agencies before its introduction in 2015.
Better: Introduced in 2015 after a lengthy consultation, the policy failed.

rules.heading: Place modifiers next to the word they modify
rules.rule: A modifier attaches to the nearest word. If that is not the word you meant, move the modifier to the right place.
rules.whenToUse: Check only, almost, nearly, just and every descriptive phrase.
structure: Only the committee approved the plan. (nobody else approved it)
The committee only approved the plan. (it approved it and did nothing more)
The committee approved only the plan. (nothing except this plan was approved)
Misplaced: The minister announced a plan to reduce emissions on Tuesday.
Fixed: On Tuesday the minister announced a plan to reduce emissions.
notes: Put only directly before the part you want to limit.
A time or place phrase at the end of a sentence attaches to the nearest noun, which is often the wrong one.

rules.heading: Keep sentences from running too long
rules.rule: Vary sentence length, but set a limit on long sentences. If a sentence goes beyond about thirty words, split it.
rules.whenToUse: When you lose track of your own sentence while writing it.
structure: Split at a coordinator: ...costs, and the delay... becomes two separate sentences.
Split at a relative pronoun: ..., which meant... becomes This meant...
Turn a clause into a phrase: Because it was expensive -> Owing to its cost
notes: Long sentences are not proof of skill; the right mix of short and long sentences is.
Two accurate sentences score higher than one heavy sentence with three errors.

examples.wrong: Due to the fact that the cost was high, the project was cancelled.
examples.right: Because the cost was high, the project was cancelled.
examples.note: Five words have become one.

examples.wrong: He almost drove his children to school every day.
examples.right: He drove his children to school almost every day.
examples.note: Almost belongs right next to every day.

examples.wrong: The committee made a decision to conduct an investigation into the matter.
examples.right: The committee decided to investigate the matter.
examples.note: Two verbs hidden inside nouns have been restored.

examples.wrong: There are a large number of students who are struggling with the course.
examples.right: Many students are struggling with the course.
examples.note: The There is... structure added no meaning.

examples.wrong: Walking through the park, the statues were impressive.
examples.right: Walking through the park, we found the statues impressive.
examples.note: Statues do not walk; the modifier needed a proper subject.

mistakes.wrong: In todays modern world of today, technology is important.
mistakes.right: Technology is now central to daily life.
mistakes.explanation: The opening phrase said the same thing twice, and important is vague.

mistakes.wrong: The report that was written by the team that was appointed last year was published.
mistakes.right: The report by the team appointed last year has been published.
mistakes.explanation: Two full relative clauses have been reduced to phrases, so the verb arrives sooner after the subject.

mistakes.wrong: She only eats vegetables on weekdays, which are organic.
mistakes.right: On weekdays she eats only organic vegetables.
mistakes.explanation: Both only and the relative clause had drifted away from the words they belonged to.

mistakes.wrong: It is important to note that it should be mentioned that costs have risen.
mistakes.right: Costs have risen.
mistakes.explanation: Neither opening phrase carries any information; delete both.

mistakes.wrong: The implementation of the utilisation of renewable resources is necessary.
mistakes.right: Renewable resources must be used more widely.
mistakes.explanation: A chain of nominalizations was hiding a simple verb. Unpack them and write a plain clause again.

keyTakeaways: Replace long stock phrases with a single word.
Keep the subject next to its verb.
Place only and every descriptive phrase right next to the word it refers to.
If you lose track of a sentence while writing it, split it.

en.intro: The final module is about judgement: choosing a register that fits the task, punctuating deliberately, and varying sentence length for effect rather than for show. Band 8 requires a wide range of structures used flexibly, and flexibility means choosing the right structure, not making everything complicated.

rules.heading: Academic and professional register
rules.rule: Formal written English avoids contractions (don't, it's), conversational phrasal verbs and addressing the reader directly as you.
rules.whenToUse: IELTS Task 1 and Task 2, reports and most official writing.
structure: No contractions: do not, cannot, it is
Avoid: get, a lot of, kids, stuff, things
Prefer: obtain or receive, a great deal of, children, factors, issues
Single-word verbs instead of phrasal verbs: find out -> discover; go up -> increase; cut down on -> reduce
No direct address: not As you can see, but As the chart shows
notes: A workplace email is less formal than an academic essay, and some contractions are normal there. Register is not one-size-fits-all; match it to the type of writing.
In formal writing, do not start sentences with And or But. Use Moreover or However, or restructure the sentence.

rules.heading: Semicolons, colons and dashes
rules.rule: Each mark has a specific job. Using the right one removes the need for extra words.
rules.whenToUse: Sparingly, and never twice in the same sentence.
structure: Semicolon - joins two closely related complete sentences: Costs rose; demand fell.
Semicolon - separates list items that already contain commas.
Colon - signals that a list, explanation or conclusion follows: Three factors matter: cost, time and access.
Dash - sets off an aside with emphasis: The result - entirely unexpected - changed the policy.
notes: A colon must follow a complete clause, not a fragment.
Use dashes sparingly in formal academic writing; they are more common in professional writing.

rules.heading: Purposeful sentence variety
rules.rule: Vary sentence length so that the structure reinforces the meaning. A short sentence after two long ones lands with force.
rules.whenToUse: At the end of a paragraph, or when stating your position.
structure: A long sentence for context and conditions...
A medium sentence to explain the point...
A short sentence for the conclusion: The cost is simply too high.
notes: Avoid three consecutive sentences of the same length and structure.
Vary sentence openings too; not every sentence has to start with the subject. An opening adverbial or participle clause changes the rhythm.

rules.heading: Aim for flexibility, not complexity everywhere
rules.rule: Good range means choosing the right structure for the job, even when that structure is simple. It does not mean every sentence has to be complex.
rules.whenToUse: In your final check before submitting any piece of writing.
structure: Ask yourself: does this sentence really need to be complex, or am I complicating it to look advanced?
Ask yourself: is every complex sentence error-free?
Ask yourself: will the reader understand it on the first read?
notes: This is where the whole course comes together: accuracy first, then complexity, then the judgement to know which to use when.

examples.wrong: There is a lot of stuff that governments can do about this.
examples.right: Governments can take a number of measures to address this.
examples.note: A vague conversational noun has been replaced with precise academic vocabulary.

examples.wrong: The policy didnt work, and it cost a lot too.
examples.right: The policy did not work, and it was expensive.
examples.note: No contraction, and a precise adjective instead of a vague quantity like a lot.

examples.wrong: Three factors matter: are cost, time and access.
examples.right: Three factors matter: cost, time and access.
examples.note: The clause before the colon must be complete, and the list follows directly.

examples.wrong: Costs rose, demand fell.
examples.right: Costs rose; demand fell.
examples.note: A semicolon joins two complete sentences where a comma cannot.

examples.wrong: As you can see from the graph, sales went up.
examples.right: As the graph shows, sales increased.
examples.note: Avoid addressing the reader directly, and use a one-word verb instead of a phrasal verb.

mistakes.wrong: In conclusion, I wanna say that governments should do more.
mistakes.right: In conclusion, governments should do more.
mistakes.explanation: Wanna is not acceptable in written English, and the lead-in phrase was unnecessary anyway.

mistakes.wrong: The main issues are: cost, time and access.
mistakes.right: The main issues are cost, time and access.
mistakes.explanation: A colon cannot separate a verb from its object; the clause before a colon must be complete.

mistakes.wrong: Costs rose; however demand fell; and prices stayed flat.
mistakes.right: Costs rose; however, demand fell and prices stayed flat.
mistakes.explanation: However needs a comma after it, and two semicolons in one sentence is excessive.

mistakes.wrong: Kids nowadays are getting addicted to their phones big time.
mistakes.right: Children today spend an increasing amount of time on their phones.
mistakes.explanation: Three register problems in one sentence: a conversational noun, a conversational verb and slang.

mistakes.wrong: Although many argue that the policy is effective, and despite the evidence, however it remains controversial.
mistakes.right: Although many argue that the policy is effective, it remains controversial.
mistakes.explanation: Three connectors for one contrast. A muddled complex sentence reads worse than a simple one.

keyTakeaways: Match the register to the task: no contractions or conversational words in academic writing.
Semicolons join sentences, colons introduce what follows, dashes emphasise an aside.
Vary sentence length and openings deliberately, especially at the end of a paragraph.
Good range means choosing the right structure, not always the most complex one.
